items.stem: Internal documentation needs one accurate sentence separating a container, the image it came from, and the Kubernetes pod that may wrap it. Which statement keeps the three straight?

options.text: The image is the read-only template, the container is one running or stopped instance created from it, and the pod is Kubernetes' unit wrapping one or more containers with shared network and storage.
options.why: Each term names a different layer: template, instance, and the Kubernetes wrapper around instances.

options.text: The container is the read-only template and the image is one running instance created from it, while the pod bundles several unrelated images together Under that framing, deleting the pod would also delete every image it happened to bundle.
options.why: This swaps the template and the instance; the image is immutable and the container is what runs from it, not the reverse.

options.text: A pod is simply another name Kubernetes uses for a container, and the image is the file produced by saving a running one Under that framing, restarting a pod would just restart the same underlying container object rather than create a new one.
options.why: A pod is a distinct Kubernetes object that can wrap several containers together; it is not a synonym for container.

options.text: Because a pod schedules its containers together, restarting one always removes and recreates the image it was built from.
options.why: Restarting a container never touches the image; the image is untouched by anything that happens to the containers created from it.

items.rationale: The image/container/pod comparison separates template, running instance, and Kubernetes wrapper. Confusing any two of them is the exam's most common trap in this section, because each concept genuinely resembles its neighbours until the cardinality and mutability are pinned down.

items.stem: A container was started ten minutes ago but no longer appears in the default output of the listing command. Which command reveals it, and why did the default view hide it?

options.text: `docker ps -a`, because bare `docker ps` shows only currently running containers by default.
options.why: The `-a` flag includes stopped containers, which the default view omits entirely.

options.text: `docker run` again with the same name, because the original process needs to be recreated from scratch.
options.why: `docker run` always creates a new container and would fail on a name collision rather than revealing the missing one.

options.text: `docker images`, because a container that stops folds back into the image store it was created from.
options.why: A container never becomes an image on its own; `docker images` lists templates, not instances.

options.text: Nothing brings it back, because a container that exits is deleted automatically the moment its process stops.
options.why: Stopping is not removing: an exited container keeps its writable layer and configuration until something explicitly removes it.

items.rationale: A container is created with `docker run` and its lifecycle state is queried with `docker ps`, whose default output filters to running containers only; `-a` includes everything, including containers whose main process already exited.

items.stem: A team wants to run a Windows-only binary inside a container on a Linux host, reasoning that containers are lightweight and portable. Why does this fail?

options.text: A container shares the host kernel rather than booting its own, so it cannot run a program built for a different OS family than the host.
options.why: There is no guest kernel to diverge from the host's, so the process must be compatible with the kernel actually running underneath it.

options.text: The registry blocks cross-platform images from being pulled onto a host running a different operating system.
options.why: A registry stores and serves images without inspecting or restricting which kernel they were built to run on.

options.text: The image's Dockerfile would need an extra `RUN` instruction to install a compatibility layer before the build succeeds.
options.why: No Dockerfile instruction changes which kernel the resulting container runs against once it starts.

options.text: Containers behave like small virtual machines, so the fix is simply to boot the container with the correct guest kernel selected, the way a hypervisor picks a guest kernel for a virtual machine.
options.why: A container has no guest kernel to select at all; the belief that it does is exactly the mistake that produces this failure.

items.rationale: Because a container is a process isolated with namespaces and cgroups on the host's own kernel, it can only run binaries compatible with that kernel. A virtual machine, by contrast, carries and boots its own kernel and can therefore run a different OS family.

items.stem: A container built from a one-shot batch script exits within a second of being started every time, and the operator suspects broken isolation. What is the more likely explanation?

options.text: The container's PID 1 process finished its work and exited, and the container's life ends exactly when that process ends.
options.why: A container exists only as long as its main process runs, so a script that completes quickly produces a container that stops quickly, by design.

options.text: The virtual machine hosting the container ran out of allocated boot time before the guest kernel could finish loading That framing assumes containers boot a guest kernel the way a virtual machine does, which is not how container isolation works.
options.why: A container has no guest kernel and no boot sequence to time out on; nothing here boots at all.

options.text: The image it was built from is corrupted, so the container cannot be created and silently fails.
options.why: A corrupted image would fail to create the container at all rather than start it and let it exit seconds later.

options.text: The cgroup limits placed on the container killed the process for exceeding its memory allowance.
options.why: An out-of-memory kill is a distinct, loggable event, not the routine behaviour of a short-lived script finishing on schedule.

items.rationale: The runtime executes the image's configured command as PID 1 inside the container's namespaces; when that process exits, the container stops immediately. A one-shot script is expected to behave exactly this way, and it is not evidence of broken isolation.

verification.reasoning: Key is correct and directly sourced: docker-overview walks through docker run and states "When you run exit to terminate the /bin/bash command, the container stops but isn't removed" -- the container's life is bounded by its main process. Distractors are all false (no guest kernel to boot, a corrupted image fails at create time, an OOM kill is a distinct event) and every why states a true fact. No double key. docker-container-ls added only because it is the reference for the resulting exited status.

items.stem: One image, dockerfile, and registry all appear in a single deployment write-up. Which pairing correctly matches recipe, artifact, and distribution point?

options.text: The Dockerfile is the recipe, the image is the built artifact produced from it, and the registry is where that artifact is stored and distributed.
options.why: Each term names a different stage: source recipe, the thing built from it, and the warehouse it is shipped through.

options.text: The image is the recipe read by the build process, and the Dockerfile is the artifact that recipe produces once built That framing reverses the build direction: nothing reads an image to produce a Dockerfile.
options.why: This reverses the two: the Dockerfile is read to produce the image, never the other way around.

options.text: The registry is the artifact itself, and the image is merely the remote server that stores registries.
options.why: The registry is the server; the image is the artifact it stores, not the reverse relationship.

options.text: An image cannot exist unless a registry currently holds it, since the local image store is only a temporary cache of registry content.
options.why: An image built locally and never pushed anywhere is still a complete, usable image; the registry is optional distribution, not a requirement for existence.

items.rationale: The Dockerfile/image/registry comparison separates recipe, built artifact, and distribution point. An image can exist purely locally with no Dockerfile in sight and no registry ever involved, which is exactly what the wrong answers deny.

options.why: It reports images on disk, which is exactly the artifact-level view the engineer needs before pruning.

options.text: `docker ps -a`, which lists every container instance so far created, running or not.
options.why: That reports instances, not the templates they were created from, and would not show unused images at all.

options.text: `docker pull`, which downloads the current state of every image the host has ever referenced.
options.why: A pull fetches one named image from a registry; it does not summarise what is already sitting locally.

items.stem: A production incident traces to an outdated dependency compiled into the application's filesystem. Which fix category does this belong to, as opposed to a wrong runtime flag?

options.text: An image problem: the dependency is baked into the layers, so it requires rebuilding, retagging and repushing before any container can pick up the fix.
options.why: A filesystem dependency is written into the image's layers, and recreating a container from the same image reproduces the same fault every time.

options.text: A container problem: stopping and starting the same container refreshes its filesystem to match whatever the image currently contains Under that framing, editing a running container's files and restarting it would silently discard the edits.
options.why: Starting a stopped container reuses the writable layer it already has; it never re-syncs against a newer version of the image.

options.text: A registry problem: the fix is to point the deployment at a different registry host that happens to carry a patched dependency.
options.why: The registry only stores whatever artifact was pushed to it; switching hosts does not change what is inside the image itself.

options.text: An environment-variable problem: setting the correct version string at run time overrides whatever the filesystem contains.
options.why: Environment variables configure the application at run time; they cannot rewrite a dependency already compiled into the filesystem.

items.rationale: Deciding whether a fix belongs to the image or the running container is the class/instance discrimination this concept exists to teach: filesystem content is an image-level fact, and only a rebuild changes it.

items.stem: Every container built from a particular image was removed with `docker rm`, yet the host's disk usage barely changed. What still occupies the space?

options.text: The image itself, which is a separate object from any container and persists on disk until something removes it directly.
options.why: Removing containers reclaims only their writable layers; the shared read-only image layers remain until the image is removed.

options.text: Nothing should remain, so the missing space is most likely an accounting delay in the disk usage tool being consulted That framing assumes the reported figures are simply stale rather than measuring genuinely different things left on disk.
options.why: The image genuinely still exists on disk; this is not a reporting artifact but the expected, documented behaviour.

options.text: Named volumes attached to those containers, which Docker never releases automatically under any circumstance.
options.why: Volumes are a separate persistence mechanism entirely, and the question describes ordinary container removal with no volumes mentioned.

options.text: Cached build context from the last time the image was built, which is stored independently of the image layers.
options.why: Build context is sent to the builder during a build and is not retained afterward as a separate disk consumer.

items.stem: A Dockerfile has, in order, `FROM`, `COPY`, `RUN`, `ENV`, `WORKDIR`, and `CMD`. Which of these instructions add a filesystem layer?

options.text: `COPY`, `RUN`, and `WORKDIR`, because each changes the filesystem, and `WORKDIR` creates its directory when it is missing.
options.why: `COPY` and `RUN` write content directly, and `WORKDIR` is the metadata-looking instruction that also creates a directory when needed.

options.text: `COPY` and `RUN` only, since every other instruction in the list is purely descriptive metadata with no filesystem effect at all.
options.why: `WORKDIR` looks like metadata but creates its target directory when that directory does not already exist, which is a real filesystem change.

options.text: `FROM`, `ENV`, and `CMD`, because they configure the image and configuration is what layers exist to record.
options.why: `ENV` and `CMD` write configuration metadata with no filesystem content, and `FROM` selects a base rather than adding a layer of its own.

options.text: All six instructions, since every line in a Dockerfile is executed in order and caches its own result as a layer.
options.why: Caching applies to every instruction, but only some of them change the filesystem; `ENV` and `CMD` cache metadata, not filesystem content.

items.stem: Two containers are attached to the same user-defined Docker network. One needs to call the other by name on its internal port, with no traffic ever coming from outside the host. Is a `-p` publish required?

options.text: No, containers on the same user-defined network reach each other directly by container name on any port, entirely without publishing.
options.why: Publishing exists to let traffic in from the host and beyond; container-to-container traffic on a shared network never needs it.

options.text: Yes, because every container port is unreachable by anything, including sibling containers, until it has been published with `-p` That framing ignores the shared user-defined network Docker Compose sets up between the project's own containers.
options.why: Publishing is specifically about host and external reachability; containers sharing a network reach each other's ports without any `-p` involved.

options.text: Yes, but only `-P` is required rather than an explicit `-p`, since `-P` covers container-to-container traffic specifically.
options.why: `-P` publishes `EXPOSE`d ports to the host the same way `-p` does; neither flag governs container-to-container traffic on a shared network.

options.text: It depends on whether the target container declared `EXPOSE` for that port in its Dockerfile.
options.why: `EXPOSE` is documentation and affects neither host publishing nor container-to-container reachability on a shared network.

items.rationale: Publishing with `-p` or `-P` is only about letting traffic in from the host and beyond. Containers attached to the same user-defined network already reach each other directly by container name on any port, with no publishing involved at all.

items.stem: An image declares `EXPOSE 80` and `EXPOSE 443`, and it is started with `docker run -P api` rather than an explicit `-p`. What happens to those two ports?

options.text: Both are published to the host, each on a separately chosen ephemeral high-numbered port rather than 80 and 443 themselves.
options.why: `-P` publishes every `EXPOSE`d port automatically, but it lets the host choose the external port rather than reusing the container's own numbers.

options.text: Both are published directly onto host ports 80 and 443, identical to writing `-p 80:80 -p 443:443` explicitly.

options.text: Neither is published, because `-P` requires a matching `-e` environment variable naming each port before it takes effect That framing invents a dependency between `-P` and environment variables that the flag does not have.
options.why: `-P` requires no accompanying environment variable; it acts directly on whatever ports the image declared with `EXPOSE`.

items.rationale: `-P` publishes every port the image declares with `EXPOSE`, each to an ephemeral high-numbered host port chosen automatically, in contrast to `-p` which lets the operator choose the exact host port for one mapping at a time.

items.stem: A database container is started with no `-v` flag, runs for weeks, and is then removed and recreated from the same image to pick up a patch. What happens to the data it wrote?

options.text: It is gone, because with no volume or bind mount attached, every write landed in the writable layer that is destroyed with the container.
options.why: Anything written outside a mounted path lives only in the container's own writable layer, which does not survive removal.

options.text: It is preserved automatically, because Docker keeps a hidden backup of every container's writable layer and restores it into any replacement container built from the same image.
options.why: Docker keeps no such backup; a writable layer is deleted along with the container that owned it, with nothing retained.

options.text: It is preserved, because the new container is created from the same image and therefore inherits the old container's filesystem state along with everything that container wrote at run time.
options.why: A new container starts from the image's layers only; it has no knowledge of, or access to, a previous container's writable layer.

options.text: It is preserved as long as the old container was stopped rather than removed before the new one was created.
options.why: The scenario explicitly removes the old container, and even a stopped-but-not-removed container's data cannot transfer to a separate new container without an explicit mount.

items.rationale: A container's writable layer exists only for the lifetime of that specific container. Without a volume or bind mount, data written inside it is destroyed the moment the container is removed, which is the single most common beginner error this concept guards against. Managed storage created ahead of time is inspected with `docker volume`.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the Docker volumes reference: "When a container is destroyed, the writable layer is destroyed with it. Using a volume ensures that the data is persisted even if the container using it is removed." With no -v the writes land in that writable layer, so removal loses them. o2 (hidden backup), o3 (image carries the previous container's run-time writes) and o4 (stopping instead of removing transfers data to a separate new container) are each false, and each why states a true fact. No two options assert the same answer. items.stem: A requirement states the host team must be able to edit application source files directly with their own editor and see changes reflected instantly inside a development container. Which choice fits, using `docker run -v`?

options.text: A bind mount, written as `-v /host/path:/path/in/container`, since it maps an existing host directory the team already edits with their own tools.
options.why: A bind mount ties the container directly to a chosen host path, which is exactly what lets an editor on the host affect files the container sees immediately.

options.text: A named volume, written as `-v pgdata:/path/in/container`, since Docker places a named volume inside the project's own source directory where the team's editor already reaches it.
options.why: A named volume lives in a location Docker manages on its own, independent of any project directory, so host edits to source files never reach it.

options.text: `docker run -e SOURCE_PATH=/host/path`, which tells the container which host directory to read source files from.
options.why: An environment variable configures the application's own settings; it cannot mount a host directory into the container's filesystem.

options.text: Rebuilding the image with `docker build` every time a source file changes, so the new content is baked in before each run.
options.why: Rebuilding on every edit defeats the instant-reflection requirement and is exactly the workflow a bind mount exists to avoid.

items.rationale: Writing the source as an existing host path in `-v source:/path/in/container` produces a bind mount, which depends on and directly reflects the host's own directory structure — ideal for mounting source code into a development container.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the bind mounts reference: "When you use a bind mount, a file or directory on the host machine is mounted from the host into a container", and its first listed use case is "Sharing source code or build artifacts between a development environment on the Docker host and a container." o2 is false — the volumes reference says a named volume "is stored within a directory on the Docker host" and is "completely managed by Docker", and "Volumes are not a good choice if you need to access the files from the host". o3 (-e mounts nothing) and o4 (rebuild per edit) are false and their whys are true. Citation defect fixed: the concept cited only docker-volumes while the key is a bind-mount claim; the bind mounts page is now cited. o2's appended "That framing ..." meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A team wants Docker itself to own and manage where data lives, rather than depending on a specific host directory layout that might differ between machines. Which mechanism fits, and why not the alternative?

options.text: A named volume, because it is created and managed by Docker in a location it owns, independent of the host's own directory structure.
options.why: A named volume's location is chosen and managed by Docker itself, so it does not depend on any particular host path existing or matching between machines.

options.text: A bind mount, because mapping an arbitrary host path is what makes storage portable across machines whose directory layouts and operating systems differ from one another.
options.why: A bind mount depends on the host's own directory structure existing at the given path, which is the opposite of portability across differently laid-out machines.

options.text: The container's own writable layer, since it is created fresh by Docker on every run without any host dependency at all.
options.why: The writable layer is destroyed with its container and is not a persistence mechanism at all, host-independent or otherwise.

options.text: An `ENV` value pointing at a data directory, letting the application decide where Docker should store its files.
options.why: An environment variable configures the application; it has no ability to create or manage storage on Docker's behalf.

items.rationale: Volumes are managed by Docker, independent of the host's own directory layout, easier to back up and migrate, and shareable between containers; bind mounts depend on the host's own structure, which is what makes them portable in the wrong direction for this requirement.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim: "While bind mounts are dependent on the directory structure and OS of the host machine, volumes are completely managed by Docker", and "When you create a volume, it's stored within a directory on the Docker host." o2 inverts that sentence and is false; o3 (writable layer as persistence) and o4 (ENV directing Docker's storage) are false, and every why states a true fact. o2's appended "on the assumption that ..." meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A container mounts a named volume at `/data`, but the application actually writes its files to `/var/lib/app`. After the container is removed and recreated, is the data still there?

options.text: No, only the mounted path is persistent; anything written to a different path inside the container still lands in the writable layer and is lost on removal.
options.why: Mounting a volume protects exactly the path it is mounted at; a path the application actually writes to elsewhere gets no protection from it.

options.text: Yes, because any volume mounted anywhere in the container protects the entire container filesystem, not just its own mount point.
options.why: A mount only covers its own path; the rest of the container's filesystem, including `/var/lib/app` here, remains part of the ordinary writable layer.

options.text: Yes, because Docker automatically detects where an application actually writes and redirects those writes into the nearest mounted volume it can find in the container.
options.why: Docker performs no such detection or redirection; a mount applies only to the exact path it was given, nothing else.

options.text: It depends on whether the volume was created with `docker volume create` in advance rather than implicitly by `docker run -v`.
options.why: How a named volume came to exist does not change which path it protects; only the mount point given at run time determines that.

items.rationale: Neither a volume nor a bind mount protects data written to some other path in the container — only the specific mounted path is persistent, which is why mounting the wrong directory silently persists nothing.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: the volumes reference describes a volume as being mounted into the container at a given directory ("When you mount the volume into a container, this directory is what's mounted into the container"), and separately that "When a container is destroyed, the writable layer is destroyed with it." A write to /var/lib/app is therefore in the writable layer and is lost. o2 (a mount protects the whole filesystem), o3 (automatic write detection) and o4 (creation method changes coverage) are false; the volumes page explicitly documents both `docker volume create` and implicit creation "during container or service creation", which is what makes o4's why true. o3's appended "That framing ..." meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: The same image needs to run unchanged in development, staging, and production, with only the database URL differing between them. What is the standard mechanism for that difference?

options.text: Environment variables set at run time with `-e`, so one image serves all three environments without any rebuild.
options.why: Run-time environment variables are exactly the mechanism for configuring an unchanged image differently per environment, without touching the image itself.

options.text: Three separate images, one built per environment with the correct database URL baked into each Dockerfile.
options.why: Baking a per-environment value into the image is exactly the anti-pattern this mechanism avoids; the requirement is one unchanged image, not three.

options.text: A different tag per environment, such as `api:dev`, `api:staging`, and `api:prod`, each pointing at differently configured builds.
options.why: A tag only names which image a reference resolves to; it does not itself carry per-environment configuration without separate builds behind it.

options.text: A bind mount pointing at a different configuration directory per environment, chosen by the host running the container.
options.why: A bind mount is designed for file-based data such as source code, not the lightweight key-value configuration a database URL represents.

items.rationale: `-e` at run time sets or overrides configuration for a single container without rebuilding the image, which is exactly what makes one image deployable unchanged across environments that differ only in settings like a database URL.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the docker container run reference, which lists `-e, --env  Set environment variables`, and the Dockerfile reference, which says values set with ENV persist into containers and you "change them using docker run --env <key>=<value>" — one image, per-run configuration, no rebuild. o2 (three images), o3 (a tag as configuration) and o4 (a bind mount as the standard mechanism for a single connection string) are each wrong for the stated requirement, and each why is true; the bind mounts page lists file-sharing use cases, not key-value configuration. Citation defect fixed: the concept cited docker-overview, whose text contains no occurrence of the phrase "environment variable" at all; it was replaced with the run CLI reference.

items.stem: A container is already running with `LOG_LEVEL=info` set by its Dockerfile's `ENV`. An operator runs `docker start web -e LOG_LEVEL=debug` hoping to change it live. What actually happens?

options.text: The command fails to apply the new value, because `docker start` has no `-e` option at all and a container's environment is fixed at the moment the container is created.
options.why: Run-time environment values are recorded at container creation; changing one requires creating a new container with `docker run -e`, not restarting the old one.

options.text: The container picks up `LOG_LEVEL=debug` immediately, since `docker start` is defined to accept the same flags as `docker run`.
options.why: `docker start` resumes an existing container using its original configuration and does not accept new run-time flags such as `-e`.

options.text: The Dockerfile's `ENV LOG_LEVEL=info` is permanently overwritten in the image, affecting every future container built from it.
options.why: Neither `docker start` nor a run-time `-e` value ever modifies the image; the image's `ENV` default is untouched by anything done to a container.

options.text: The container restarts with a fresh writable layer, discarding whatever it had written before, because a changed setting forces the container to be rebuilt from its image.
options.why: `docker start` never resets a container's writable layer; the described failure is that the new flag has no effect at all, not that data is lost.

items.rationale: `ENV` in a Dockerfile writes a default every container from that image inherits; `-e` at run time overrides it for one container, but only at creation. Because those values are fixed once a container exists, `docker start` cannot apply a new one.

The key claimed `docker start` "accepts no new flags", which the docker container start reference disproves: it documents -a/--attach, -i/--interactive, --detach-keys, --checkpoint and --checkpoint-dir. What that page does not list is any -e/--env option, which is the true reason the operator's command cannot work; the key now says exactly that. With the key corrected, o2 (start takes docker run's flags) is false against the same option table, o3 (the image's ENV overwritten) is false against the Dockerfile reference, and o4 (writable-layer reset) is false against the start reference, and each why states a true fact. Citation defect fixed: docker-overview was cited and contains nothing about `docker start` or environment variables. o4's appended "That framing ..." meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A developer sets a database password with `-e DB_PASSWORD=...` instead of hardcoding it in application code, reasoning this keeps it out of sight. Is the credential now safe?

options.text: No, an `-e` value is ordinary container configuration that anyone able to inspect the container can read, so it is no better protected than any other setting.
options.why: Environment variables are ordinary configuration, visible to anything that can inspect the container, which is a weaker guarantee than the developer assumed.

options.text: Yes, because environment variables are encrypted by the container runtime the moment the container starts.
options.why: Neither `ENV` nor `-e` values are encrypted by the runtime; both are stored and readable as plain configuration.

options.text: Yes, but only because `-e` values are discarded from memory once the application process finishes reading them at startup.
options.why: A `-e` value remains part of the container's recorded configuration for its whole lifetime; it is not discarded after the application first reads it.

options.text: No, but only because the value should have been baked in with `ENV` in the Dockerfile instead, which is the genuinely secure form.
options.why: An `ENV` default is part of the image and readable by anyone who can pull it, which is more widely exposed than a run-time `-e` value, not less.

items.rationale: Neither `ENV` nor `-e` is a secret store: an `ENV` value is baked into the image and readable by anyone who can pull it, and a `-e` value is readable from the container's configuration on the host. Real secrets belong in a dedicated secret manager instead.

items.stem: An image's Dockerfile sets `ENV TIMEOUT=30`, and a container is run with `docker run -e TIMEOUT=60 api`. Which value does the application see?

options.text: 60, because a run-time `-e` value overrides whatever default the image's `ENV` instruction baked in.
options.why: The run-time override always wins for that one container; the image's `ENV` is only the fallback used when no `-e` is given.

options.text: 30, because a value set inside the Dockerfile is treated as fixed configuration that a run-time flag cannot change.
options.why: An image's `ENV` is a default, not a lock — `-e` at run time is specifically designed to override it for that container.

options.text: Neither value, because setting the same variable in two places causes Docker to refuse to start the container.
options.why: Docker resolves the conflict by letting the run-time value win; it does not refuse to start over a variable being set twice.

options.text: Both, concatenated as `30,60`, since Docker merges duplicate environment variable definitions rather than choosing one.
options.why: Docker does not merge duplicate variable values; the run-time `-e` value simply replaces the image's default for that container.

items.rationale: `ENV` in the Dockerfile writes a default every container inherits; `-e` at run time sets or overrides a value for that one container, and the run-time value takes precedence whenever both are given.

items.stem: A container exited five minutes ago with an error. Which diagnostic step still works, and which does not?

options.text: `docker logs` still works, because it replays the already-captured stdout and stderr stream; `docker exec -it` does not, because it needs a running process to join.
options.why: Logs are a replay of a captured stream that survives the process exiting, while exec starts a new process inside one that must already be running.

options.text: Neither works once a container has exited, since both diagnostic commands require the container to still be running.
options.why: `docker logs` specifically works on an exited container because it reads a captured stream rather than talking to a live process.

options.text: `docker exec -it` still works on an exited container as long as `-t` allocates a fresh terminal for it.
options.why: Allocating a terminal does not create a process to run inside; exec always needs a running container to attach its new process to.

options.text: Both work identically, because Docker keeps an exited container's filesystem on disk and queryable, which is all that either of the two commands needs in order to run.
options.why: An exited container's filesystem being on disk does not make it possible to start a new process inside it; exec still requires a live main process.

items.rationale: Diagnostic order matters: `docker logs` reads the captured stdout/stderr stream and works on a container that has already exited, while `docker exec -it` needs a running process to join and does not.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed on both halves. The exec half is explicit: "The docker exec command runs a new command in a running container. The command you specify with docker exec only runs while the container's primary process (PID 1) is running." The logs half rests on the json-file driver page — "By default, Docker captures the standard output (and standard error) of all your containers, and writes them in files using the JSON format" — plus the logs CLI page, which describes the command as one that "batch-retrieves logs present at the time of execution" and imposes no running-container requirement: the stream is read back from stored files, not from a live process. o2, o3 and o4 are each false against those two pages and each why is true. Citation defect fixed: the whole concept cited only docker-overview, which mentions neither `docker exec` nor `docker attach` nor any logging driver. o4's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: An application inside a container writes its own log file to `/var/log/app.log` instead of standard output, and `docker logs web` shows nothing useful. What is the fix, and which command exposes the problem?

options.text: Reconfigure the application to log to stdout and stderr; `docker exec -it web sh` can confirm the file exists inside the container while the platform never sees it.
options.why: The stdout/stderr convention is what `docker logs` reads; a file written inside the container is invisible to it and disappears when the container is removed.

options.text: Run `docker logs -f` instead of the plain form, since `-f` widens what the command reads to include log files written anywhere inside the container's own filesystem, not just its output stream.
options.why: `-f` only follows the same captured stdout/stderr stream live; it does not search the container's filesystem for log files.

options.text: Mount a volume at `/var/log` so the file becomes visible to `docker logs` automatically once it is outside the writable layer.
options.why: A volume makes a path persistent across container recreation, but it does not make `docker logs` read arbitrary files; that command only ever reads the captured output stream.

options.text: Set `-e LOG_PATH=/var/log/app.log` so the runtime knows where to redirect the captured stream from.
options.why: An environment variable configures the application, not what `docker logs` reads; the platform always captures stdout and stderr regardless of any such setting.

items.rationale: Containers deliberately have no journal or syslog by convention, so applications are expected to log to stdout and stderr, which the platform captures. A file written inside the container is invisible to `docker logs` and lost when the container is removed.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: "By default, Docker captures the standard output (and standard error) of all your containers, and writes them in files using the JSON format" — a file the application writes itself is never part of that capture, so the fix is to log to stdout/stderr, and `docker exec` ("runs a new command in a running container") is what lets you confirm the file exists inside. o2 is false against the logs CLI page, which scopes --follow to "the new output from the container's STDOUT and STDERR"; o3 is false because a volume changes persistence, not what the logging driver captures; o4 is false because capture is a daemon-side behaviour no application variable redirects. Every why states a true fact. Citation defect fixed (docker-overview replaced). o2's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A container's logging driver is configured to ship output to a remote system, and `docker logs` is run against it locally. What should be expected?

options.text: Unless that cache is explicitly disabled, it generally still works, because Docker Engine keeps a local cache of the stream even under a remote driver.
options.why: Dual logging keeps a local copy alongside whatever a remote driver does, so `docker logs` continues to function in the ordinary case.

options.text: It always fails outright, because a remote logging driver replaces the local capture entirely with no exceptions.
options.why: A remote driver does not categorically replace local capture; Docker Engine's dual logging keeps a local cache in the ordinary case.

options.text: It returns the container's entire filesystem contents instead of just the captured output stream, since the remote driver changes what is read.
options.why: `docker logs` only ever reads the captured stdout/stderr stream, never the filesystem, regardless of which driver is configured.

options.text: It requires `docker exec -it` to be run first to establish a connection to the remote logging system before logs can be read.
options.why: `docker logs` and `docker exec -it` are independent commands; neither is a prerequisite for the other under any logging driver configuration.

Docker Engine uses the local logging driver to act as cache for reading the latest logs of your containers. This is called dual logging." The same page carries a "Disable the dual logging cache" section, which is exactly the exception the key's trailing clause names, so the key is neither overstated nor unqualified. o2 (always fails), o3 (returns the filesystem) and o4 (exec as a prerequisite) are each false, and each why is true. Citation defect fixed: docker-overview was cited and contains no mention of logging drivers at all.

items.stem: A candidate uses `docker attach` to a running container's main process instead of `docker exec -it`, and a stray Ctrl-C stops the container entirely. What distinguishes the two commands?

options.text: `docker attach` connects a terminal to the existing main process, so signals reach it directly; `docker exec` starts a separate new process instead.
options.why: Because attach shares the main process's own input stream, a signal like Ctrl-C is delivered to that process itself, which can terminate the container.

options.text: Both commands behave identically, and the container would have stopped regardless of which one was used.
options.why: An exec session runs an additional process separate from the main one, so a Ctrl-C there terminates only that additional process, not the container.

options.text: `docker attach` only works on stopped containers, so the described scenario could not have actually involved it.
options.why: `docker attach` requires a running container, since it connects to that container's live main process; it does not work on a stopped one.

options.text: `docker exec -it` is the one that connects to the container's existing main process, while `docker attach` is the one that starts an additional shell alongside it.
options.why: This reverses the two: `docker exec` starts a new process, while `docker attach` connects to the existing main process.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against both CLI pages. Attach: "Attach local standard input, output, and error streams to a running container" ... "it will forward signals ... To stop a container, use CTRL-c" (with --sig-proxy true by default sending SIGINT to the container). Exec: "runs a new command in a running container" whose command "only runs while the container's primary process (PID 1) is running" — a separate process, so a signal there does not reach PID 1. o2 (identical behaviour), o3 (attach on stopped containers) and o4 (the two swapped) are false, and each why is true; o3's why is directly supported by attach's "to a running container". Citation defect fixed: docker-overview does not mention either command. o4's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A web API container holds no data of its own and pushes everything to an external database, while a message-queue container stores its messages on local disk. How should these two be classified?

options.text: The API is stateless, so any instance can serve any request and is freely replaceable; the queue is stateful and needs persistent storage and careful handling.
options.why: Statelessness is about whether an instance owns data that must outlive it; the API pushes its state outward while the queue keeps its own.

options.text: Both are stateless, because neither one runs a database engine directly inside its own container.
options.why: Owning data on local disk is what makes a workload stateful, regardless of whether that data lives in a dedicated database engine.

options.text: Both are stateful, because every container writes something to its own writable layer while it runs.
options.why: Writing to a writable layer during normal operation does not make a workload stateful; what matters is whether data must survive the instance being replaced.

options.text: The API is stateful because it depends on an external database, and the queue is stateless because messages in transit are transient and never need to outlive the instance holding them.
options.why: Depending on an external stateful service does not make the dependent instance itself stateful, and messages stored on local disk are exactly the kind of data that must survive the instance.

items.rationale: A stateless container keeps nothing that has to outlive it and is freely interchangeable; a stateful container owns data that must survive it and therefore needs persistent storage and, usually, a stable identity.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the CNCF glossary's own term pages. Stateless Apps: "Stateless applications handle each request independently without remembering any previous interactions or user data." Stateful Apps: "state refers to any data the app needs to store to function as designed ... stateful apps needs some kind of storage that is accessible from anywhere." The API pushes its state to the database and is stateless; the queue owning messages on local disk is stateful. o2, o3 and o4 are false against those definitions and each why states a true fact. CITATION DEFECT, the predicted CNCF hazard, confirmed again: the concept cited https://glossary.cncf.io/ , whose fetched body is a tag index and a project blurb — it defines no term at all and contains neither "stateless" nor "stateful" outside the browse-by-tag list. Replaced with the two per-term pages. o4's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A team plans to handle rising load on a stateful workload the same way they scale their stateless API — simply run more replicas. Why does this not work as cleanly?

options.text: Scaling a stateful workload is a data problem, not a scheduling one, since each replica would need its own persistent storage and possibly a stable identity.
options.why: Horizontal scaling assumes interchangeable replicas; a stateful workload's replicas are not interchangeable because each owns data the others do not.

options.text: It works identically for both, since replicas of any workload become fully interchangeable with one another as soon as they are started from the same container image.
options.why: Sharing an image says nothing about whether replicas share or duplicate data; a stateful workload's replicas remain distinct by the data they hold.

options.text: It fails because stateful workloads cannot be containerized at all and must run directly on bare metal.
options.why: Stateful workloads run in containers routinely, provided they are given persistent storage; containerization itself is not the obstacle.

options.text: It fails because Docker enforces a hard limit of one replica per stateful container, unlike stateless ones.
options.why: There is no such enforced replica limit; the real obstacle is that additional replicas each need their own persistent storage and coordination, not a platform-imposed cap.

items.rationale: Horizontal scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing all assume replicas are indistinguishable, which is true by design for stateless workloads. A stateful workload's replicas each need their own persistent storage, which is why scaling it is a data problem rather than simply adding more copies.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the Kubernetes StatefulSet page, which supplies both halves of the key precisely: pods "are created from the same spec, but are not interchangeable: each has a persistent identifier that it maintains across any rescheduling", and StatefulSets serve applications requiring "Stable, unique network identifiers" and "Stable, persistent storage". The CNCF stateful-apps page adds that such apps "need some kind of storage that is accessible from anywhere". o2 is refuted by the same "created from the same spec, but are not interchangeable" sentence; o3 (stateful workloads cannot be containerized) is false — the StatefulSet API exists for exactly that; o4 invents a Docker replica cap. Each why is true. Citation defect fixed (cncf-glossary landing page replaced). o2's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: An on-call engineer kills a misbehaving instance of a service without checking anything first, trusting the platform to recover. For which kind of workload is that trust well placed by default?

options.text: A stateless one, where killing one instance costs nothing but in-flight work, since any other instance can serve the same requests.
options.why: Statelessness is exactly the property that makes an instance disposable — nothing it uniquely held is lost by killing it.

options.text: A stateful one, since persistent storage automatically makes a workload resilient to any instance being killed at will.
options.why: Persistent storage protects the data, but killing a stateful instance without checking anything can still cause data loss or downtime depending on how it manages that storage.

options.text: Either kind equally, since the orchestrator recreates any killed instance the same way regardless of what it holds.
options.why: Recreating an instance says nothing about whether the data it uniquely held survives; that is exactly the distinction between the two kinds of workload.

options.text: Neither kind, since killing any running instance without warning always risks losing in-flight requests regardless of statelessness.
options.why: In-flight work is a minor, expected cost either way; the distinction that decides whether the trust is well placed is whether irreplaceable data is also at risk.

items.rationale: The whole point of a stateless workload is that killing any one instance costs nothing durable — any other instance is equally capable of serving the same requests, which is exactly what self-healing and freewheeling replacement rely on.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: the CNCF stateless-apps page says such applications "handle each request independently without remembering any previous interactions or user data", and the StatefulSet page's contrast — "If an application doesn't require any stable identifiers or ordered deployment, deletion, or scaling, you should deploy your application using a workload object that provides a set of stateless replicas" — is the disposability the key names. o2 is false: persistent storage protects the data, not the workload's tolerance of an abrupt kill, and the StatefulSet page documents ordered, graceful handling for exactly that reason. o3 and o4 are false, and each why states a true fact. Citation defect fixed (cncf-glossary landing page replaced). o4's why referred to "this concept", a pointer to the study material from inside the item; reworded.

items.stem: A candidate claims Docker is the container runtime that actually creates and runs containers on a Kubernetes node. Is that accurate?

options.text: No, Docker is a full toolchain layered above a runtime; containerd and CRI-O are the components a Kubernetes node typically uses to actually run containers.
options.why: The runtime is the lower-level piece that does the actual work; Docker adds a CLI, image building, and networking on top of one.

options.text: Yes, and from the release that removed dockershim onward Kubernetes stopped supporting any cluster that does not run Docker specifically as the runtime on every one of its worker nodes.
options.why: Kubernetes talks to a runtime through the Container Runtime Interface and supports containerd, CRI-O, and other implementations; it never required Docker specifically.

options.text: Yes, and images built with any other tool cannot run under containerd or CRI-O as a result.
options.why: Images produced by Docker are ordinary OCI images and run unmodified under containerd or CRI-O; the OCI specifications exist precisely to guarantee this.

options.text: No, and the actual runtime is the registry that images are pulled from before a node can start them.
options.why: A registry only stores and distributes images; it plays no role in actually creating or running a container process on a node.

items.rationale: Docker is a full toolchain — CLI, image building, networking, volume management — layered above a runtime. The runtime itself is the component, typically containerd or CRI-O on a Kubernetes node, that actually creates and runs the container process.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim in the Kubernetes cluster architecture page: "Container runtime ... Kubernetes supports container runtimes such as containerd, CRI-O, and any other implementation of the Kubernetes CRI (Container Runtime Interface)." The dockershim page adds the layering the key asserts: "on each node, the kubelet uses the container runtime interface as an abstraction so that you can use any compatible container runtime." o2 is refuted by the same sentences; o3 is refuted by the dockershim page's "If you are using Docker for building your application containers, you can still run these containers on any container runtime"; o4 (registry as runtime) is plainly false. Each why is true. o2's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: An image built on a laptop with Docker runs unmodified under containerd on a cluster node with no changes needed. What makes that portability guaranteed rather than lucky?

options.text: The Open Container Initiative's Image, Runtime, and Distribution specifications, which keep images and runtimes from different vendors interchangeable.
options.why: Portability here is a specification the tools conform to, not a coincidence of two particular products happening to agree with each other.

options.text: Docker Hub silently converts every pushed image into a containerd-specific format before that image can be pulled down onto a cluster node running a different runtime.
options.why: No such conversion happens; an image is stored and served as the same OCI-compliant artifact regardless of which registry hosts it.

options.text: Kubernetes rebuilds every image from its Dockerfile the first time it is scheduled onto a new node.
options.why: Kubernetes never rebuilds images; it pulls the already-built artifact and hands it to the node's runtime to run as-is.

options.text: The node's kubelet translates the image's layers into a Kubernetes-native format before the runtime can use them.
options.why: The kubelet drives the sequence of pulling and running through CRI, but it does not translate or reformat the image; the runtime consumes standard OCI layers directly.

items.rationale: The OCI's Runtime, Image, and Distribution specifications are what keep an image built with one tool running unmodified under another; the portability claim is a specification being honoured, not marketing.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim on the OCI about page: "The OCI currently contains three specifications: the Runtime Specification (runtime-spec), the Image Specification (image-spec) and the Distribution Specification (distribution-spec)", formed "for the express purpose of creating open industry standards around container formats and runtimes", with the distribution spec introduced "to standardize the API to distribute container images". Naming all three is what makes the key exact rather than approximate. o2 (registry-side format conversion), o3 (Kubernetes rebuilding from Dockerfiles) and o4 (kubelet reformatting layers) are each false; the OCI page's description of an implementation downloading an OCI image and unpacking it into a runtime bundle leaves no room for a translation step, and each why is true. o2's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A team hears that "Kubernetes dropped Docker" and worries their Docker-built images will stop working on newer clusters. Is that concern justified?

options.text: No, Kubernetes changed which runtime component it talks to directly, but images produced by Docker remain standard OCI images and run there without change.
options.why: The change affects the low-level runtime interface Kubernetes uses, not the image format, so nothing about a Docker-built image itself stops working.

options.text: Yes, because dropping Docker means the cluster can no longer read images built anywhere except with containerd's own build tool.
options.why: The image format is OCI-standard regardless of which build tool produced it; the runtime change concerns how Kubernetes runs containers, not what it can read.

options.text: Yes, and every image will need to be repushed to a containerd-specific registry before it can be pulled again.
options.why: Registries store OCI images regardless of runtime; nothing about a runtime change requires repushing to a different kind of registry.

options.text: No, because Kubernetes never had any hand in running containers in the first place, so no change it makes to its own components could affect image compatibility either way.
options.why: Kubernetes does drive container execution through a runtime via the kubelet; the accurate reassurance is about image portability, not that nothing was ever running.

items.rationale: Kubernetes talks to a runtime through the Container Runtime Interface and supports containerd, CRI-O, and other CRI implementations. Images produced by Docker remain ordinary OCI images and run there without change — the runtime interface changed, not the image format.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim: "Kubernetes' built-in dockershim component was removed in release v1.24 ... If you are using Docker for building your application containers, you can still run these containers on any container runtime. This use of Docker does not count as a dependency on Docker as a container runtime." o2 and o3 are refuted by that same sentence plus the OCI page's image-spec, and o4 is false because the same page states Kubernetes does drive execution — "on each node, the kubelet uses the container runtime interface as an abstraction" — so the reassurance it offers is the wrong one. Each why is true. Citation defect fixed: the item cited only the OCI about page, which never mentions Kubernetes, dockershim or CRI; the Kubernetes dockershim page is now cited. o4's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A dozen containers, defined together with their networks and volumes, run happily through Docker Compose on one developer's laptop. A colleague calls this "orchestration for small deployments." What is the actual dividing line between Compose and an orchestrator?

options.text: How many hosts are involved and whether anything keeps watching afterward: Compose applies a file to one machine once, an orchestrator schedules across many and keeps reconciling.
options.why: The number of containers is not the discriminator; Compose happily runs a dozen. Hosts and continuous reconciliation are what actually separate the two.

options.text: The number of containers involved — Compose is meant for a handful, while an orchestrator is required once a dozen or more are running.
options.why: Compose has no such container-count limit; a dozen containers on one host is well within its normal use, and container count is not what makes something an orchestrator.

options.text: Whether the containers are described declaratively — Compose is imperative, while an orchestrator always requires declarative YAML.
options.why: A Compose file is itself declarative, describing services, networks and volumes to be created; declarativeness is not what separates it from an orchestrator.

options.text: Whether the containers were built from a Dockerfile — Compose only runs pre-built images, while an orchestrator can build them too.
options.why: A Compose file can reference a build context the same way a plain `docker build` can; build capability is not the dividing line described here.

items.rationale: Compose and an orchestrator are a named confusable pair, and the dividing line is hosts plus persistence of intent: Compose applies a file to one machine once, while an orchestrator schedules across a fleet and keeps reconciling afterward — not how many containers are involved.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed on both halves. Compose's own "Why use Compose?" page scopes it to one machine — its production section is titled "Single host deployments" and reads "Compose supports production deployments on single hosts" — while the CNCF container-orchestration page supplies the continuous half: an orchestrator lets users "declare how it should look like" and "will then automatically monitor the infrastructure and correct it if its state deviates from the declared one (e.g., spin up a new container if one crashes)". o2 is false because neither page mentions any container count; o3 is false because a Compose file is itself a declaration of services, networks and volumes; o4 is false because Compose files may carry a build context. Each why is true. Citation added: the reconciliation half of the key had no source before.

items.stem: A project's Compose file defines a web service, a worker service, and a shared database, and `docker compose up -d` is run. What creates, and in what relationship?

options.text: It creates the network, volumes, and containers for all three services on the single host where the command ran, starting anything they depend on as it goes, and detaches immediately.
options.why: `-d` runs it detached; Compose brings up every declared service together on that one machine, respecting the dependencies declared between them.

options.text: It distributes the three services across whichever machines in the local network have spare capacity, balancing the load automatically.
options.why: Compose is a single-host tool; every service in the project runs on the one machine where the command was issued, with no cross-host distribution.

options.text: It only creates the containers, leaving the operator to run `docker volume create` and attach each declared mount by hand afterwards for everything else the Compose file happens to describe.
options.why: Compose creates the network and volumes declared in the file as part of the same command, not as a separate manual step.

options.text: It builds fresh images for all three services from their Dockerfiles every time, regardless of whether anything changed.
options.why: `docker compose up` reuses existing images unless a rebuild is requested with `--build`; it does not rebuild unconditionally on every invocation.

items.rationale: `docker compose up` creates the network, volumes, and containers declared in the file, in dependency order, all on the single host the command runs on; `-d` detaches so the shell returns immediately while the services keep running.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as written, then fixed. The key said "in dependency order" for a stem that declares no dependencies; the Compose up reference supports the weaker and accurate "Unless they are already running, this command also starts any linked services", which the key now mirrors. The rest of the key is confirmed: up "Builds, (re)creates, starts, and attaches to containers", "Running docker compose up --detach starts the containers in the background and leaves them running", and the down reference's "removes containers, networks, volumes, and images created by up" establishes that up is what created the network and volumes. o2 is false against the single-host scoping on Compose's own overview page; o3 is refuted by that same down sentence; o4 is false because up "picks up the changes by stopping and recreating the container" only when configuration or image changed, and --build exists for forcing a rebuild. Each why is true. o3's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A machine running a Compose project loses power overnight, and the project declares no restart policy for any of its services. What happens to the application when it comes back, if no one intervenes?

options.text: It stays down, because Compose has no cross-host scheduling or automatic rescheduling after a host failure; nothing was watching to bring it back.
options.why: Compose applies the file once when the command is run; once that machine is gone, nothing external notices or reacts on its own.

options.text: It resumes automatically on the same machine, since Compose registers a restart policy with the host's boot process by default.
options.why: Compose configures no such automatic boot-time recovery by default; nothing restarts the project unless the operator runs the command again.

options.text: It migrates to another machine on the network automatically, since Compose treats every Docker host it can reach as one interchangeable pool to place services into.
options.why: Compose has no concept of a pool of hosts at all; it is bound to the single machine where the command was run.

options.text: It resumes only the database service, since Compose prioritizes services declared with persistent volumes over stateless ones.
options.why: Compose applies no such prioritization on its own; without the command being run again, nothing in the project restarts regardless of which services declare volumes.

items.rationale: Compose has no cross-host scheduling and no rescheduling after a host failure: if the machine dies, the application dies with it, and nothing brings it back until the command is run again — the exact gap an orchestrator is built to close.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as written, then fixed. The original stem left the restart policy unstated, which made o2 arguable — a service declaring `restart: always` genuinely does come back when the daemon starts — so the item had two defensible answers. The stem now rules that out explicitly and the key is unambiguous. Key confirmed: Compose's overview page scopes the tool to "Single host deployments" and describes it as applying a file ("you can create and destroy these environments in just a few commands"), with nothing in it or in the up reference that watches a host or reschedules after failure. o2 is false as a default claim, o3 is false because Compose has no notion of a host pool at all, and o4 invents a per-service prioritisation. Each why is true. o3's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: An operator stops a Compose project with `docker compose stop` instead of bringing it down, then wonders why the network and containers are still visible in `docker ps -a`. What is the distinction?

options.text: Stopping halts the containers without removing them or the network; only bringing the project down deletes the containers and network it created.
options.why: Stop and down are different operations, mirroring the container-level distinction between stopping and removing.

options.text: There is no distinction, and both commands are expected to remove the containers and network identically.
options.why: Stopping a project merely halts it; only bringing it down removes the containers and network, so the two commands are not interchangeable.

options.text: The visibility in `docker ps -a` is a stale cache and will clear itself automatically within a few minutes regardless of which command was used.
options.why: The containers genuinely still exist after a stop; this is not a caching artifact but the expected state of a stopped, unremoved container.

options.text: Stopping only affects services that declare a database volume, leaving stateless services running as before.
options.why: Stopping a project halts every service it declares, regardless of whether that service is stateless or stateful.

items.rationale: Stopping a Compose project halts its containers, mirroring `docker stop`; bringing it down removes the containers and network it created, mirroring `docker rm`. The two are not interchangeable, exactly as at the single-container level.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim from the two CLI references. stop: "Stops running containers without removing them. They can be started again with docker compose start." down: "Stops containers and removes containers, networks, volumes, and images created by up", with "Containers for services defined in the Compose file" and "The default network, if one is used" among the things removed by default. o2 is refuted by that pair directly; o3 is false because the containers genuinely still exist; o4 invents a volume-dependent scope for stop, which the stop page's single -t/--timeout option and blanket wording exclude. Each why is true. Citation added: the concept previously cited only the Compose overview page, which describes neither command.

items.stem: A developer argues that running an application as root inside a container is harmless "because it is only a container." Why is that the wrong instinct?

options.text: Because the kernel is shared with the host, the isolation boundary a compromised root process must cross is thinner than a hypervisor's, so the consequences reach further than in a VM.
options.why: Shared-kernel isolation is weaker than a hypervisor boundary, which is exactly why root privileges inside a container carry more real risk than the phrase suggests.

options.text: It is not wrong, since the namespaces a container is started with make root inside that container fully equivalent to an ordinary unprivileged user account on the host machine itself.
options.why: Namespaces narrow what a process can see, but they do not eliminate the shared-kernel attack surface a root process can still reach.

options.text: Because a registry automatically rejects any image that was built and run as root, making the practice self-correcting.
options.why: A registry stores whatever it is pushed and performs no inspection of which user an image runs as.

options.text: Because running as root disables the image's declared `EXPOSE` ports, leaving the application unreachable.
options.why: The user a process runs as has no effect on port publishing; `EXPOSE` and `-p` are unrelated to the container's user.

items.rationale: Container isolation is weaker than a virtual machine's because the kernel is shared, so a compromise inside a container that runs as root reaches further than the same compromise would inside a VM — the practical answer is running as a non-root user, not adding a scanner at the end.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim in NIST SP 800-190 section 3.5.2: "although containers provide strong software-level isolation of resources, the use of a shared kernel invariably results in a larger inter-object attack surface than seen with hypervisors, even for container-specific OSs. In other words, the level of isolation provided by container runtimes is not as high as that provided by hypervisors." Docker's build best practices supplies the countermeasure the stem is about — "If a service can run without privileges, use USER to change to a non-root user" — and NIST 3.1.2 names the defect: "an image may not be configured with a specific user account to run as and thus run with greater privileges than needed." o2 is refuted by that same NIST sentence; Docker Engine security says only that "Namespaces provide the first and most straightforward form of isolation", never equivalence to an unprivileged host user. o3 and o4 are false and their whys true. CITATION DEFECT FIXED: the concept cited only docker-build-best-practices, whose fetched text contains zero occurrences of "hypervisor" and one of "kernel" — it cannot support the key's central comparison. NIST SP 800-190 added. o2's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A registry credential is passed into a build with `ARG`, and a later Dockerfile instruction unsets the variable before the image is finished. Is the credential safe once the build completes?

options.text: No, it is still present in the layer where it was written, and unsetting it later does not erase it; it must never enter a layer in the first place.
options.why: A layer records history rather than current state, so a value written and then unset is still readable from the earlier layer that recorded it.

options.text: Yes, because unsetting a build argument removes that value from every layer of the finished image, not only from the single layer in which the value was last read during the build.
options.why: Layers are additive history; unsetting a variable in a later instruction changes the final metadata but does not retroactively remove it from the earlier layer.

options.text: Yes, but only if the base image was pinned to a specific version rather than left unpinned.
options.why: Pinning the base image's version affects reproducibility of the build, not whether an `ARG` value persists in a layer once written.

options.text: It depends on whether the credential was also set with `ENV` in addition to `ARG`, since only `ENV` values persist in layers.
options.why: Both an `ARG` value used during the build and an `ENV` default persist in the image's layers or configuration; using `ARG` alone does not make it safe.

items.rationale: A value passed through `ARG` or set with `ENV` persists in the image and can be recovered from it even if a later instruction unsets it, because layers record history and nothing erases an earlier one — the only reliable approach is to never write a secret into a layer at all.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim on Docker's build secrets page: "Build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they persist in the final image. Instead, you should use secret mounts or SSH mounts, which expose secrets to your builds securely" — the key's "it must never enter a layer in the first place" is exactly that instruction. o2 is refuted by the same sentence; o3 (base-image pinning) and o4 (only ENV persisting) are false, and o4's why is true precisely because the source names build arguments and environment variables together. Each why states a true fact. Citation added: docker-build-best-practices mentions ARG but does not state the persistence rule the key turns on. o2's appended meta-clause was rewritten into the distractor's own voice.

items.stem: A team believes a one-time vulnerability scan performed when an image was first built is sufficient going forward. What is missing from that plan?

options.text: Scanning needs to be continuous, because vulnerabilities are discovered later in images that have not themselves changed at all.
options.why: A scan reflects known vulnerabilities at the moment it runs; new ones are disclosed over time against unchanged software, so a single scan goes stale.

options.text: Nothing is missing, since a base image that passed a scan once can never later be found vulnerable without the image itself changing.
options.why: New vulnerabilities are regularly disclosed in already-published software, so an unchanged image can become newly flagged with no rebuild involved.

options.text: The scan should have been run against the Dockerfile's text instead of the built image, since vulnerabilities live in instructions, not artifacts.
options.why: Vulnerabilities are found in the software packages inside the built image, not in the Dockerfile text describing how it was assembled.

options.text: The scan needs to be run once per container created from the image rather than once per image, since each container has its own writable layer.
options.why: Vulnerabilities live in the shared image layers, not in any single container's writable layer, so scanning per-container adds nothing a single image-level scan does not already cover.

items.rationale: Scanning is a continuous activity rather than a one-off, because vulnerabilities are discovered in images that have not changed at all — a smaller, version-pinned base image reduces what there is to find, but does not remove the need to keep checking.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim in NIST SP 800-190 section 3.1.1: "An image created with fully up-to-date components may be free of known vulnerabilities for days or weeks after its creation, but at some time vulnerabilities will be discovered in one or more image components, and thus the image will no longer be up-to-date." Section 4.1.1 prescribes the continuous form — tools with "Integration with the entire lifecycle of images, from the beginning of the build process, to whatever registries the organization is using, to runtime." o2 is refuted by the 3.1.1 sentence; o3 is false because 3.1.1 locates the vulnerabilities in image components, not in the Dockerfile text; o4 is false because those components live in the shared image layers. Each why is true. CITATION DEFECT FIXED: docker-build-best-practices was cited and its fetched text contains no vulnerability-scanning guidance at all (its only "scan" hits are unrelated site navigation).

items.stem: A production fleet needs to survive a node failure, scale up under load, and roll out new versions without downtime. A single-host Compose setup already runs the containers involved. What is missing, and why does adding more containers to the same host not fix it?

options.text: Orchestration across a pool of hosts with continuous reconciliation: the requirement is about surviving a host failure and rescheduling, which a bigger single host cannot provide.
options.why: The discriminating property is many hosts plus a controller that keeps comparing actual state to desired state, not how many containers run on one machine.

options.text: More containers on the same host, since orchestration is fundamentally about running a far larger number of containers than a Compose project on one machine was ever designed to handle.
options.why: Container count is not the discriminator; the requirement is surviving a host failure, which no number of containers on one host can satisfy.

options.text: A bigger base image with more resources allocated per container, so each one can absorb more load individually.
options.why: Resource allocation per container does not address a host dying entirely, which removes every container on it regardless of how well-resourced each one was.

options.text: A faster registry, so that images pull more quickly whenever the single host needs to restart a container.
options.why: Pull speed does not create the additional hosts, scheduling, or health-checking that surviving a node failure and scaling under load require.

items.rationale: The exam's alternative answer to an orchestration requirement is always a single-host tool, usually Compose. The discriminating property is multiple hosts plus continuous reconciliation — something that keeps comparing running state against declared state and acts on the difference indefinitely, which a single, larger host still cannot provide.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. The CNCF container-orchestration page gives the reconciliation half: orchestration tools "allow users to determine a system's state. First, they declare how it should look like ...
