items.stem: A node running several workloads stops reporting heartbeats to the orchestrator. What happens to the workloads that were running on it?

options.text: They are recreated elsewhere, because nodes are watched the same way workloads are, and a node that stops reporting has its workloads rescheduled rather than left stranded.
options.why: Continuous reconciliation applies to node health too, not only to individual workload health, so a lost node's work is moved rather than abandoned.

options.text: They stay assigned to that node indefinitely, since an orchestrator reacts only to a workload's own process crashing and has no view of whether a node is still reporting in.
options.why: Nodes are health-checked the same way workloads are; a node that stops reporting triggers rescheduling of its workloads onto healthy nodes.

options.text: They are paused rather than recreated, waiting for a human operator to manually confirm the node is actually down.
options.why: Reconciliation acts automatically once a node is detected as unhealthy; it does not wait on a manual confirmation step before rescheduling.

options.text: They are removed permanently, since an orchestrator treats a lost node as a signal to reduce the declared replica count.
options.why: A lost node does not change what was declared; the orchestrator still works to satisfy the same declared count by scheduling replacements elsewhere.

items.rationale: Nodes are watched the same way individual instances are: a node that stops reporting has its workloads recreated elsewhere instead of left stranded, which is exactly the self-healing property a single-host tool cannot offer.

items.stem: A CI pipeline builds an image, pushes it, and submits an updated declaration to the cluster. Weeks later, a pod crashes and is replaced automatically. Which component is responsible for that replacement?

options.text: The orchestrator, because what keeps the declaration true afterward is the orchestrator's continuous reconciliation, not the pipeline that ran once at deploy time.
options.why: A pipeline runs and finishes; the orchestrator is what keeps comparing actual state to desired state indefinitely, long after the pipeline has stopped running.

options.text: The CI pipeline, since it is triggered automatically to rerun whenever any workload in the cluster crashes.
options.why: A pipeline builds and pushes; it plays no role in detecting a crashed workload weeks after it last ran and has no ongoing connection to the cluster's runtime state.

options.text: The registry, because it revalidates every image it has served on a fixed schedule and triggers a replacement whenever one of those scheduled checks comes back failing.
options.why: A registry only stores and serves images on request; it has no scheduling role and does not trigger replacements for crashed workloads.

options.text: The container runtime on the node, acting entirely on its own without any coordination from a cluster-level component.
options.why: The runtime on a node executes what it is told, but deciding to recreate a crashed workload and where to place it is the orchestrator's reconciliation logic, not an independent runtime decision.

items.rationale: Orchestration is not CI/CD: a pipeline builds the image, pushes it, and may submit the updated declaration, but what keeps that declaration true for the weeks afterward — including replacing a crashed workload — is the orchestrator, continuously reconciling.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the Kubernetes controllers page: "In Kubernetes, controllers are control loops that watch the state of your cluster, then make or request changes where needed. Each controller tries to move the current cluster state closer to the desired state", introduced through the thermostat analogy of desired versus current state — a non-terminating loop, which is what distinguishes it from a pipeline that ran once. The CNCF orchestration page states the same behaviour concretely: the tool will "automatically monitor the infrastructure and correct it if its state deviates from the declared one (e.g., spin up a new container if one crashes)." o2, o3 and o4 are each false and each why is true. items.stem: Someone claims the orchestrator itself is what starts container processes and isolates them, the same way a runtime does. What is wrong with that claim?

options.text: Orchestration is not a runtime: the orchestrator decides what should run where, while the runtime on each node is what actually starts and isolates the container.
options.why: Deciding placement and starting a process are different layers of responsibility, and collapsing them is exactly the confusion the claim commits.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since the orchestrator and the runtime are simply two names for the same underlying component.
options.why: They are distinct layers with distinct jobs — scheduling and reconciliation versus actually creating and isolating the process — not two names for one thing.

options.text: It is wrong only because orchestration also does not build or push images, which is a separate and unrelated gap in the claim.
options.why: That is a true additional gap, but it does not address the specific runtime-versus-orchestrator confusion the claim actually makes.

options.text: It is wrong only because orchestration operates on pods rather than on individual containers, which makes the whole disagreement a Kubernetes-specific matter of vocabulary.
options.why: That distinction is real but separate; the claim's core error is conflating the orchestrator's scheduling role with the runtime's execution role.

items.rationale: Orchestration is not a runtime and not containerization: the orchestrator decides what should run where, and the runtime on each node actually starts it, isolated with namespaces and cgroups, from an image that already exists.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed by a single sentence that splits the two layers exactly as the key does: "Kubernetes is responsible for orchestration and scheduling of Pods; on each node, the kubelet uses the container runtime interface as an abstraction so that you can use any compatible container runtime." items.stem: A statement describes Kubernetes as "governed by the CNCF, which also hosts it." Is that the correct relationship?

options.text: No, the CNCF hosts Kubernetes as a graduated project, but governance rests with Kubernetes' own Steering Committee, an elected body its charter names as the project's governing authority.
options.why: Hosting and governing are separated deliberately: the CNCF provides funding, infrastructure, and marketing support, while technical and community direction stays with the project's own structures.

options.text: Yes, since a graduated CNCF project is by definition directly governed by the foundation that hosts it.
options.why: Graduation describes hosting maturity, not governance; Kubernetes' own Steering Committee, not the CNCF, is named as its governing body.

options.text: No, because Kubernetes is not hosted by the CNCF at all, but by the Linux Foundation directly instead.
options.why: The CNCF, itself part of the Linux Foundation, is specifically the body that hosts Kubernetes as a graduated project.

options.text: Yes, and the Steering Committee referenced elsewhere is simply an internal CNCF department with no independent authority, treating hosting and governance as the same relationship rather than two deliberately separated ones.
options.why: The Steering Committee is Kubernetes' own elected governing body, distinct from and not subordinate to the CNCF's internal structure.

items.rationale: Two facts about Kubernetes' standing are routinely confused and both are examinable: it is hosted by the CNCF as a graduated project, and it is governed by its own Steering Committee — the CNCF hosts, funds, and supports; it does not govern.

options.text: Vocabulary and purpose, meaning recognising what Kubernetes is for and naming its core objects, not operational skill such as writing manifests.
options.why: LFCA depth stays at recognition and understanding, deliberately stopping short of the hands-on skill a CKA-level assessment would require.

options.text: Full manifest-writing ability, since LFCA and CKA test the exact same depth of Kubernetes operational skill.
options.why: LFCA and CKA target different depths; LFCA stops at recognition and purpose, while CKA-level operational skill is explicitly out of scope here.

options.text: No Kubernetes knowledge at all, since the Containers competency confines itself entirely to single-host Docker concepts.

items.stem: Someone draws an analogy between the CNCF's relationship to Kubernetes and the Linux Foundation's relationship to the Linux kernel. Is that comparison sound?

options.text: Yes, both foundations host and fund the project without setting its technical direction, which stays with the project's own governance structures.
options.why: The Linux Foundation describes itself as a non-profit providing a neutral home plus support programs for marketing, events, infrastructure and training, and the CNCF charter says hosted projects keep their existing technical governance; the shape is the same in both cases.

items.stem: A candidate is asked to place cluster, node, pod, and container in a containment hierarchy from largest to smallest. What is the correct order?

options.text: A cluster contains nodes, a node runs pods, and a pod holds containers.
options.why: Each layer contains the next: the cluster is the whole pool of machines, a node is one machine, and a pod is the unit of containers running on it.

options.text: A node contains clusters, a cluster runs pods, and a pod holds containers.
options.why: This reverses the cluster and the node; a cluster is the larger pool that a node belongs to, not the other way around.

options.text: A cluster contains pods directly, and nodes are an optional layer that some clusters omit entirely.
options.why: Every cluster needs at least one worker node in order to run pods at all; a node is not an optional layer.

options.text: A pod contains nodes, and a node runs directly inside a container.
options.why: This inverts the entire hierarchy; a node is a machine that runs pods, not something contained inside one.

items.rationale: Node, pod, and container form a containment hierarchy the exam expects a candidate to keep straight: a cluster contains nodes, a node runs pods, and a pod holds containers.

verification.reasoning: Key is verbatim doctrine on the cluster-architecture page: a Kubernetes cluster consists of a control plane plus a set of worker machines, called nodes, that run containerized applications, and the worker nodes host the Pods that are the components of the application workload; the Pods page supplies the last level, a Pod is a group of one or more containers. o2 inverts cluster and node. o3 is refuted verbatim by Every cluster needs at least one worker node in order to run Pods, which is also exactly what its why claims. o4 inverts the whole hierarchy. items.stem: A new pod remains stuck in a not-starting state, and every node in the cluster is already running workloads near its resource limit. What level does this problem resolve to?

options.text: The node level, because no node has enough spare resource capacity for the scheduler to place the pod, which is exactly the constraint it schedules against.
options.why: The scheduler places workloads against node capacity, so "why is this pod not starting" frequently resolves to insufficient room on the available nodes.

options.text: The registry level, since a pod that cannot start is always evidence that the image it references failed to be pulled from the registry named in its manifest.
options.why: The scenario describes nodes already at their resource limit, not a failed pull; a registry problem would surface differently.

options.text: The container level, since the pod's individual containers must each be resized before the pod as a whole can be scheduled.
options.why: Scheduling decides which node a pod goes to as a whole; resizing individual containers inside it does not address the described lack of node capacity.

options.text: The Service level, since a stable network endpoint must exist before the scheduler will place any pod behind it.
options.why: A Service governs addressing after pods exist; it is not a prerequisite the scheduler checks before placing a pod on a node.

items.rationale: Node capacity is what the scheduler places workloads against, so a pod stuck not starting frequently resolves to a node-level answer — insufficient resources, or no node matching the pod's constraints.

verification.reasoning: Confirmed only after rewrite; the defect found as authored, the fix, and the re-check are all recorded here. Content confirmed, shape defect found and fixed. The key is supported by the cluster-architecture page: kube-scheduler watches for newly created Pods with no assigned node and selects a node for them to run on, and the first listed factor is individual and collective resource requirements, so no-room-on-any-node is precisely the constraint it schedules against. o2, o3 and o4 are each false and each why states a true fact (a failed pull surfaces as an image error, the scheduler places whole pods, and a Service addresses pods that already exist rather than gating their placement). The defect: o3 ran two sentences together with no full stop, appending a meta-clause that merely paraphrased its own why. That pattern appears on 43 of 258 distractors in this file and on 0 of 86 keys, so it is a mechanical tell a reader could score on without knowing any Kubernetes. Removed the appended clause; the content it carried already lives in the why.

items.stem: A node running several pods that belong to Deployments is drained for maintenance. What happens to those pods, and why is this considered safe?

options.text: They are recreated on other nodes, which is safe only because pods are treated as disposable and their replacements can serve requests just as well.
options.why: Draining relies on pod disposability; a replacement pod on another node is expected to be functionally equivalent to the one it replaces.

options.text: They pause in place on the draining node and resume there once maintenance finishes, since draining marks a node unschedulable without moving the pods already running on it.
options.why: Draining specifically causes a node's pods to be recreated elsewhere so maintenance can proceed without leaving workloads stranded on it.

options.text: They are deleted permanently, since draining is treated identically to scaling the replica count down to zero.
options.why: Draining moves workloads to other nodes rather than reducing any declared count; the pods are recreated, not permanently removed.

options.text: They are converted into a Service so that traffic can continue reaching the maintenance node directly.
options.why: A Service is an addressing abstraction in front of pods; draining a node has no effect that converts a pod into one.

items.rationale: Nodes are replaceable: draining one causes its pods to be recreated elsewhere, which is only safe because pods are treated as disposable rather than as irreplaceable, hand-tended processes.

verification.reasoning: Confirmed only after rewrite; the defect found as authored, the fix, and the re-check are all recorded here. Refuted as authored. The item is entirely about kubectl drain and it cited only the cluster-architecture page, which does not contain the word drain. Re-sourced to the Safely Drain a Node task page, you can use kubectl drain to safely evict all of your pods from a node before you perform maintenance on the node, and to the Pods page, which supplies both halves of the key: Pods are designed as relatively ephemeral, disposable entities, and if a Node fails, a controller notices that Pods on that Node have stopped working and creates a replacement Pod, the scheduler places the replacement Pod onto a healthy Node. Second defect: the stem said only several running pods, which made o3 (deleted permanently) genuinely defensible, because a bare pod evicted by a drain is not recreated by anything. Tightened the stem to pods belonging to Deployments, which closes that second reading. items.stem: A scaling request asks for "five instances" of a service. One engineer interprets this as five pods; another as five containers inside one pod. Which is the Kubernetes model, and why does it matter?

options.text: Five pods, since the scheduler places pods, never containers directly, so scaling means creating more pods, not adding more containers to one.
options.why: Kubernetes manages pods, not containers directly, so scale-out is expressed entirely in terms of the number of pods, not containers packed into one.

options.text: Five containers inside one pod, since a pod is simply Kubernetes' name for a larger container that can hold several processes.
options.why: A pod is not a bigger container; it is a distinct wrapper, and adding more containers to one pod is a co-location decision, not a scaling one.

options.text: Either interpretation is equally correct, since the scheduler treats containers and pods as interchangeable units of placement.
options.why: The scheduler places pods specifically; it has no mechanism for placing individual containers independently of the pod that wraps them.

options.text: Five Deployments, one per instance, since each running copy of the service needs its own separate Deployment object.
options.why: A single Deployment already declares a replica count and manages that many pods from one pod template; five separate Deployments would be redundant.

items.rationale: This is the distinction most often missed: the scheduler places pods, not containers, so a pod's containers can never be split across two nodes, and scaling always means creating more pods, never adding more containers to one pod.

verification.reasoning: Confirmed only after rewrite; the defect found as authored, the fix, and the re-check are all recorded here. Content confirmed, shape defect found and fixed. The Pods page settles the key twice over: Kubernetes manages Pods rather than managing the containers directly, and if you want to scale your application horizontally you should use multiple Pods, one for each instance, which in Kubernetes is typically referred to as replication. o2 is false, a Pod is a group of one or more containers with shared namespaces rather than a larger container, and its why is true. o3 is false and its why is true. o4 is false and its why is true, since one Deployment declares .spec.replicas and manages that many pods from a single template. Defect fixed: o3 ran two sentences together with no full stop, appending a paraphrase of its own why.

items.stem: A pod holds a main application container and a sidecar container that must share the main container's network so it can inspect traffic on `localhost`. Why does putting both in one pod satisfy that requirement?

options.text: Containers in the same pod share a network namespace, one IP address and one port space, so they reach each other over `localhost` by design.
options.why: Pod-level network sharing is exactly the mechanism that lets two tightly coupled containers talk to each other without any external routing.

options.text: Because Kubernetes automatically creates a Service between any two containers placed in the same pod.
options.why: A Service addresses a set of pods from outside, not two containers within the same pod; pod-internal reachability comes from the shared network namespace itself.

options.text: Because every container in a cluster can already reach every other container over `localhost`, regardless of which pod holds it, extending pod-scoped network sharing to the whole cluster.
options.why: Localhost reachability is scoped to containers sharing the same pod's network namespace; it does not extend cluster-wide between unrelated pods.

options.text: Because both containers were built from the same image, which is what grants them a shared network namespace.
options.why: Network namespace sharing is a property of pod membership, not of whether two containers happen to come from the same image.

items.rationale: Containers in a pod share a network namespace, meaning one IP address and one port space between them, which is exactly why a sidecar that must share the main container's network belongs in the same pod rather than a separate one.

verification.reasoning: Key is verbatim doctrine on the Pods page: every container in a Pod shares the network namespace, including the IP address and network ports, and within a Pod containers share an IP address and port space and can find each other via localhost. The page's own phrase Inside a Pod (and only then) supplies the scope limit that refutes o3 directly. o2 is false, nothing creates a Service between containers of one pod, and the Service page confirms a Service addresses a set of pods from outside rather than containers within one. o4 is false, namespace sharing follows from pod membership, and the page's own sidecar example pairs two containers built from different images. All three whys state true facts, no distractor is defensible, and no two options assert the same answer.

items.stem: A failing pod is replaced automatically. Is the replacement the same pod, repaired, or something else?

options.text: Something else; pods are ephemeral, so a failing one is not repaired but replaced by a new pod with a new name and a new IP address.
options.why: Kubernetes treats pods as disposable rather than long-lived: replacement, not repair, is the mechanism.

options.text: The same pod, repaired in place, since Kubernetes preserves a pod's identity and IP address across any failure it recovers from.
options.why: A pod's replacement is a genuinely new pod with a new identity and IP; pods are not repaired and resumed the way a stopped container can be.

options.text: The same pod, but only its IP address changes while its name and configuration stay identical to before the failure.
options.why: Both the name and the IP address change on replacement; nothing about the failed pod's identity is preserved.

options.text: A different pod entirely, created on the same node the failed one was running on, since replacement never crosses node boundaries.
options.why: A replacement pod can be scheduled onto any node with capacity; nothing ties it to the specific node the failed pod happened to run on.

items.rationale: Pods are ephemeral: a failing pod is not repaired but replaced, and the replacement is a new pod with a new name and a new IP address — which is exactly why addressing a pod directly is a bug waiting for the next restart.

verification.reasoning: Confirmed only after rewrite; the defect found as authored, the fix, and the re-check are all recorded here. Refuted as authored on sourcing. The key asserts that the replacement gets both a NEW NAME and a NEW IP ADDRESS, and the only cited page, Pods, supports the new address (it calls the pod an ephemeral network identity and says a controller creates a replacement Pod, which the scheduler places onto a healthy Node) but never says anything about the replacement's name. Added k8s-deployment, whose worked example shows the pods a ReplicaSet creates named nginx-deployment-75675f5897-7ci7o, that is DEPLOYMENT-NAME plus pod-template-hash plus a random suffix, so a replacement necessarily carries a different name. Re-checked after the fix: o2 is false, a pod is not repaired and resumed, the doc's mechanism is replacement; o3 is false because it claims the SAME pod survives, which no reading supports, so it is not a second key even for a StatefulSet (whose sticky per-ordinal naming is out of scope for this bank, which has no StatefulSet concept); o4 is false and its why is true, the Pods page says the scheduler places the replacement onto a healthy Node with no tie to the failed pod's node. Each why states a true fact. Also fixed a shape defect: o4 ran two sentences together with no full stop, appending a paraphrase of its own why.

items.stem: A bare pod is created directly through the Kubernetes API, with no Deployment involved. What limitation does this carry compared to a pod created by a workload controller?

options.text: Nothing keeps a declared count of it, and nothing recreates it if it fails, since a bare pod has no controller reconciling toward a desired replica count.
options.why: A Deployment is what watches and maintains a pod count; a bare pod exists as a one-off with no such supervision behind it.

options.text: It cannot share a network namespace between its own containers the way a Deployment-created pod can, so its containers must reach each other over the cluster network instead.
options.why: Network namespace sharing between containers is a property of the pod itself, present whether or not a workload controller created it.

options.text: It cannot be scheduled onto a node at all, since only Deployment-created pods are eligible for scheduling.
options.why: The scheduler places any pod regardless of how it was created; a bare pod is scheduled the same way a Deployment-created one is.

options.text: It automatically becomes a Deployment after its first restart, adopting a replica count of one.
options.why: A bare pod never converts into a Deployment on its own; without one explicitly created, nothing supervises the pod at all.

items.rationale: Bare pods are rarely created directly — a workload controller such as a Deployment is normally what creates them, because it is the controller that watches and maintains a declared replica count; a bare pod has no such supervision and is not recreated if it fails.

verification.reasoning: Confirmed only after rewrite; the defect found as authored, the fix, and the re-check are all recorded here. Content confirmed, shape defect found and fixed. The Pods page carries the key: usually you do not need to create Pods directly, even singleton Pods, and workload resources and their controllers are what implement application scaling and auto-healing, so a bare pod has nothing reconciling toward a declared count. o2 is false, network namespace sharing is a property of the pod and is present however the pod was created, and its why says exactly that. o3 is false, the same page says the new Pod is scheduled to run on a Node whether it was created directly by you or indirectly by a controller. o4 is false, nothing promotes a pod into a Deployment. Defect fixed: o3 ran two sentences together with no full stop, appending a paraphrase of its own why.

items.stem: Deployment, Kubernetes service, and pod all appear in a change request describing a rolling update. Which statement correctly assigns each object's role?

options.text: The Deployment governs how many pods and which version, the Service governs how callers address them, and the pod is where the containers actually run.
options.why: Each object answers a different question: lifecycle and version, stable addressing, and actual execution.

options.text: The Service governs how many pods and which version, and the Deployment only selects existing pods by label without creating anything, swapping which object owns replica count and which one owns addressing.
options.why: This swaps the two roles: the Deployment creates ReplicaSets and declares the replica count, while the Service selects existing pods and creates nothing.

options.text: The pod governs how many replicas should exist, and the Deployment is merely where the containers physically run.

items.stem: A workload needs a stable per-instance identity and its own dedicated storage that must not be shared across replicas. Is a Deployment the right object for it?

options.text: No, a Deployment assumes interchangeable, essentially stateless pods, and a workload needing stable identity and per-instance storage is not its job.
options.why: The Deployment model treats its pods as freely replaceable copies of each other, which conflicts directly with a requirement for per-instance identity.

options.text: Yes, since a Deployment can be configured to assign a fixed identity to each of its replicas by setting the replica count to a specific value and leaving it unchanged thereafter.

items.stem: A frontend calls a backend by directly recording one of its pod IP addresses. After a routine redeploy, the frontend cannot reach the backend at all. What is the fix, and why does it hold up across future redeploys?

options.why: A Service exists precisely because pod IPs are ephemeral; addressing through it means a redeploy never breaks the caller.

options.text: Pin the backend's Deployment to always reuse the exact same pod IP address on every redeploy, so recording it once remains valid.
options.why: Pod IPs are assigned fresh on each replacement and are not something a Deployment can pin to a fixed value across redeploys.

options.why: A volume solves data persistence, not address stability; nothing about a shared volume tracks which pods are currently ready to serve traffic.

items.stem: A service needs to be reachable from the public internet through a provider-managed load balancer. Which Service type fits, as opposed to the cluster-internal default?

options.text: LoadBalancer, which exposes the Service externally through a load balancer, typically provisioned by the cloud provider — unlike ClusterIP, the default that stays internal only.
options.why: LoadBalancer is specifically the type built for external exposure; ClusterIP is deliberately unreachable from outside the cluster.

options.text: ClusterIP, since it is the default type and a default is always the safest starting point for an exposure requirement.

options.why: NodePort exposes a port on each node directly, which is a different mechanism from a provider-managed external load balancer, even though both allow outside traffic in.

options.why: That setting concerns which network namespace a pod uses, not how external clients discover a stable address; it is not the standard mechanism for external exposure.

options.text: No, pods already running on healthy nodes keep serving; what stops is new scheduling, updates, and any other change to cluster state.

options.why: Whether a pod is managed by a Deployment or created bare has no bearing on whether it keeps running during a control plane outage; both keep serving on their nodes.

options.why: Cluster DNS and Service resolution are not what fails during a brief control plane outage in this scenario; the accurate distinction is scheduling and changes stopping while running workloads continue.

items.stem: A candidate must name the control plane component that watches for newly created pods with no assigned node and picks one for them. Which is it?

options.text: `kube-scheduler`, which selects a node for each unscheduled pod based on its declared resource needs and placement constraints.
options.why: Choosing a node for a pod with no assignment is precisely the scheduler's defined responsibility among the four control plane components.

options.text: `kube-apiserver`, which is the front end for the Kubernetes API and therefore also performs node selection for every pod.
options.why: The API server is the front end for the Kubernetes control plane and exposes the Kubernetes API, but it does not select a node for a pod; that is the scheduler's job.

options.text: etcd, since it stores all cluster data and therefore also decides which node a new pod is assigned to.
options.why: etcd is the consistent key-value store backing cluster data; it stores decisions made elsewhere but does not itself decide node placement.

options.text: `kube-controller-manager`, which runs the controller processes and therefore also handles new-pod scheduling as one of its controllers.
options.why: The controller manager runs reconciliation controllers for existing objects; assigning a node to a newly created, unscheduled pod is the scheduler's separate, dedicated job.

items.stem: A team decides to back up only their application data volumes, reasoning that cluster configuration can always be reapplied from source control. Which single control plane component still deserves its own backup, and why?

options.text: etcd, because it is the one stateful control plane component, holding the cluster's actual recorded state rather than something rederivable from manifests alone.

items.stem: Which statement correctly places the CNCF relative to the Linux Foundation and to Kubernetes?

options.text: The CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation and hosts Kubernetes as one of its graduated projects, providing infrastructure, events, and marketing rather than technical direction.
options.why: This places the CNCF correctly within the Linux Foundation and correctly separates hosting support from governing authority over Kubernetes.

options.text: The CNCF is the parent organisation of the Linux Foundation, and Kubernetes is therefore governed directly by the CNCF's own board rather than by any elected committee belonging to the project.
options.why: The relationship runs the other way — the CNCF is part of the Linux Foundation, not its parent — and Kubernetes is governed by its own Steering Committee regardless.

options.text: The CNCF hosts only the Linux kernel, while Kubernetes is hosted by a separate and unrelated foundation with no Linux Foundation ties.
options.why: The CNCF's portfolio is the cloud-native ecosystem, Kubernetes included; the Linux kernel is a Linux Foundation project hosted separately from the CNCF's own portfolio.

options.text: The CNCF is a for-profit vendor consortium that owns the trademarks of every open source project it hosts, Kubernetes included.
options.why: The CNCF is a nonprofit foundation whose mission is making cloud native computing ubiquitous, not a for-profit vendor consortium.

items.rationale: The Cloud Native Computing Foundation is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation and hosts a large portfolio of vendor-neutral open source projects, Kubernetes among them, sustaining the ecosystem with infrastructure, events, and marketing rather than technical governance.

verification.reasoning: Confirmed only after rewrite; the defect found as authored, the fix, and the re-check are all recorded here. Refuted as authored on sourcing. The key asserts that Kubernetes is one of the CNCF's GRADUATED projects, and neither cited page states a maturity level for any project. Added cncf-project-kubernetes: Kubernetes was accepted to CNCF on March 10, 2016 at the Incubating maturity level and then moved to the Graduated maturity level on March 6, 2018. The rest of the key is sourced where it was: CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation and hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure and runs the largest open source developer conferences (Who-we-are), while the charter assigns marketing, events and project productivity infrastructure to the foundation and says in section 8(c) that included projects continue under their existing technical governance. o3 is false, the Linux kernel is not a CNCF project. o4 is false, the CNCF's mission is to make cloud native computing ubiquitous under the nonprofit Linux Foundation; note the trademark half of o4 is actually TRUE (charter section 11 requires a project to transfer trademark and logo assets to the Linux Foundation or a project hosting entity), but the option is a conjunction whose for-profit vendor consortium half is false, so it is not a second key, and its why correctly targets the false half. Second defect fixed: o2 ran two sentences together with no full stop, appending a paraphrase of its own why.

items.stem: A candidate reads a question naming both an organisation and a project it hosts, and correctly suspects it is testing whether they collapse hosting and governing into one role. What is the safest general answer to that kind of question?

options.text: State the hosting relationship and the separate governing body explicitly, rather than assuming the host also directs the project technically.
options.why: The CNCF charter says projects included in the CNCF continue to run through their existing technical governance structure, and the Kubernetes Steering Committee charter names that committee the governing body of the project, so the two roles are held by two different bodies and are stated separately.

options.text: Assume the named organisation both hosts and governs, since a foundation prominent enough to host a project of that size usually also directs its technical roadmap.
options.why: The CNCF charter states that included projects continue under their existing technical governance structure, so hosting a project does not carry technical direction with it.

options.text: Assume the project governs itself entirely with no relationship to any hosting organisation at all.
options.why: The hosting relationship is real and examinable — funding, infrastructure, and marketing support genuinely come from the host — so denying it entirely is also wrong.

options.text: Treat the question as unanswerable without knowing the specific committee names involved.
options.why: The relationship can be stated correctly without naming an individual: the CNCF hosts and funds, while the project's own elected Steering Committee governs.

items.rationale: This is the same shape as the Linux Foundation's relationship to the Linux kernel, and a question that names one organisation and one project is usually probing whether the candidate collapses the two roles into one — naming hosting and governing as distinct answers it correctly.

Second, k8s-steering-charter was added to source_ids, since the governing-body half of the key was carried by neither cited page. Third defect fixed: o2 ran two sentences together with no full stop. Re-checked: o3 is false, the hosting relationship is real, and o4 is false, the shape is statable without any committee membership.

items.stem: A new open source project applies to join the CNCF's portfolio. What does progressing from sandbox to graduated status actually represent?

options.text: Demonstrated adoption and governance maturity, tracked by the CNCF as hosting stages, not a transfer of technical direction to the foundation.
options.why: Graduation reflects how mature and adopted a project has become under CNCF hosting criteria; it says nothing about who directs the project technically.

options.text: The point at which the CNCF takes over day-to-day technical decisions from the project's own maintainers.
options.why: Day-to-day technical authority stays with each project's own maintainers and governance structures regardless of hosting stage.

options.text: A rebranding step in which the project's name and trademark transfer fully to Linux Foundation ownership.
options.why: Graduation is a hosting-maturity classification, not a trademark or naming transfer event of that kind.

options.text: The moment a project is required to switch its container runtime to containerd and adopt the CNCF's own release cadence as a condition of remaining hosted.
options.why: Hosting stage has no bearing on which container runtime a project uses; the CNCF imposes no such technical requirement as a condition of graduation.

items.rationale: Projects enter at sandbox level and progress through incubating to graduated as adoption and governance maturity are demonstrated; a Technical Oversight Committee maintains the foundation's technical vision, while day-to-day technical authority stays with each project's own maintainers.

verification.reasoning: Confirmed only after rewrite; the defect found as authored, the fix, and the re-check are all recorded here. Refuted as authored on sourcing, and this is the sharpest instance of the pattern in my range. The item is entirely about the CNCF's sandbox-to-graduated ladder, and it cited cncf-who-we-are and cncf-charter. Who-we-are does not contain the words sandbox, incubating or graduated at all; the charter's only occurrence of any of them is the incidental phrase non-sandbox project maintainers in the TOC election clause. Added cncf-project-kubernetes, which names the levels as levels (accepted at the Incubating maturity level, moved to the Graduated maturity level), and cncf-graduation-application, the TOC template a project files to graduate, which requires an adoption assertion listing adopting organisations plus a completed Governance Review and General Technical Review, which is precisely the adoption and governance maturity the key claims and contains nothing transferring technical direction to the foundation. Reached that template through process/graduation_criteria.md, which now only forwards to it, so the older graduation-criteria URL is itself citation rot. Re-checked: o2 is false, the template asks a project to demonstrate its own governance rather than surrender it; o3 is false, graduation is not a trademark event (the charter's trademark transfer is an inclusion requirement, not a graduation one); o4 is false and its why is true. Second defect fixed: o4 ran two sentences together with no full stop.
